issues.legal_issue: A law providing for permanent acquisition of land for town planning is not exempt from the constitutional requirements governing compulsory acquisition merely because it promotes public health.
material_facts: The scheme provided for land needed by the local authority to vest in it when the final scheme came into force.
The town-planning legislation was intended to promote planned urban development, sanitation, and healthier living conditions.
issues.conclusion: The vesting of land needed by the local authority constituted compulsory acquisition, and the law was not exempt from the requirements governing compulsory acquisition on the ground that it promoted public health.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 31(2), compulsory acquisition must be for a public purpose and under a law providing compensation and either fixing its amount or specifying the principles and manner for determining and giving it. The public-health exception in Article 31(5)(b)(ii) does not cover permanent acquisition of property merely because its object is to promote public health. Deputy Commissioner and Collector, Kamrup v. Durga Nath Sarma was followed.

predicates.town_planning_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns a law providing for acquisition of land as part of a town-planning scheme.
predicates.property_vests_in_public_body: The law provides that land needed for a public body vests in that body.

issues.definition: When a town-planning acquisition provides for needed land to vest in a public body, the public-health purpose does not make the acquisition exempt.

issues.legal_issue: A compulsory-acquisition law satisfies the compensation guarantee when it specifies relevant, non-illusory valuation principles, and the resulting amount cannot be challenged merely as inadequate.
material_facts: The legislation adjusted compensation and contributions by comparing the market value of original and reconstituted plots at the date of the declaration of intention to make the scheme.
If an owner received no reconstituted plot, the legislation provided for payment of the value of the original plot using that same valuation date.
The owner challenged the valuation method because it did not provide a just equivalent at the time the owner's interest was extinguished, which occurred many years after the declaration of intention.
issues.conclusion: The legislation specified relevant principles for determining compensation, and the compensation was not illusory. The challenge that the resulting compensation was not a just or adequate equivalent could not invalidate the law.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as amended by the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, bars judicial review of compensation for inadequacy when the law fixes compensation or specifies principles for determining it. A court may still examine whether the stated principles are irrelevant or whether the supposed compensation is illusory. The Court treated observations in P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector as obiter and overruled Union of India v. Metal Corporation of India Ltd.; it also explained the earlier approach in State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee and State of West Bengal v. Subodh Gopal Bose in light of the amendment.

rule.if: compulsory_acquisition_compensation_case and legislature_set_uniform_valuation_rule and valuation_rule_relevant and compensation_not_illusory and challenge_claims_inadequacy

predicates.compulsory_acquisition_compensation_case: The proceeding challenges compensation provided for a compulsory acquisition.
predicates.legislature_set_uniform_valuation_rule: The legislature prescribed a general valuation rule for determining what an affected owner is to receive.
predicates.valuation_rule_relevant: The prescribed valuation rule bears a rational relation to determining compensation.
predicates.compensation_not_illusory: The compensation produced by the prescribed rule is not merely nominal or fictitious.
predicates.challenge_claims_inadequacy: The challenger argues that the compensation is inadequate or not a just equivalent.

issues.definition: If a compensation challenge concerns a relevant general valuation rule that produces non-illusory compensation, a claim of inadequacy does not invalidate that rule.

issues.legal_issue: An earlier valuation date or a harsh result in a particular case does not invalidate an acquisition law on the ground of unreasonableness.
material_facts: The legislation valued land by reference to the date when the intention to make the scheme was declared, rather than the later date when the scheme came into force and the owner's interest was extinguished.
A substantial period elapsed between the declaration of intention and the scheme coming into force.
issues.conclusion: The elapsed time and the use of the earlier valuation date did not invalidate the legislation on the ground of unreasonableness or because it operated harshly in the particular case.
issues.legal_principle: A law providing for compulsory acquisition under Article 31(2) cannot be challenged as imposing unreasonable restrictions under Article 19(1)(f). The validity of the law does not depend on whether it operates harshly in a particular case. Smt. Sitabati Debi v. State of West Bengal was followed.

predicates.acquisition_law_challenge: The proceeding challenges the validity of a law providing for compulsory acquisition.
predicates.compensation_uses_earlier_valuation_date: The law determines compensation by reference to a date earlier than the date the owner's interest is extinguished.
predicates.challenge_alleges_unreasonableness_or_ha: The challenger relies on the valuation method or its harsh operation in the particular case to allege unreasonableness.

issues.definition: When an acquisition-law challenge relies on an earlier valuation date and alleges unreasonableness or a harsh result, those circumstances do not invalidate the law.

issues.legal_issue: A town-planning acquisition does not deny equal protection merely because its compensation method differs from the method used for a separate government acquisition, where the local authority has no choice between methods for the town-planning acquisition.
material_facts: The town-planning legislation prescribed the method for determining compensation for land subject to a town-planning scheme.

A separate acquisition procedure was available for land acquired by the State Government, but the local authority had no option to use that procedure instead of the town-planning legislation for scheme land.
issues.conclusion: The compensation provisions did not violate the guarantee of equality before the law or equal protection of the laws.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 is not infringed by different compensation procedures where the local authority is required to use the procedure prescribed for town-planning acquisitions and has no arbitrary choice between alternative methods for the same acquisition. The Court distinguished P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector, where the State could choose between acquisition procedures without legislative guidance, and applied Taylor v. Taylor.

predicates.town_planning_acquisition_case: The proceeding concerns an acquisition carried out through a town-planning scheme.
predicates.local_authority_has_mandatory_procedure: The local authority is required to use the procedure prescribed for acquisitions under the scheme.
predicates.no_arbitrary_choice_between_methods: The local authority cannot choose among alternative methods for carrying out the same scheme acquisition.

issues.definition: When a town-planning acquisition must follow a prescribed procedure and the local authority has no arbitrary choice of method, a difference from a separate acquisition procedure does not defeat the equality challenge.
